name: Analytical Marxism
summary: Analytical Marxism is a school, active from the late 1970s, that restates Marx's questions about history, class and exploitation with the methods of analytical philosophy, rational-choice theory and neoclassical economics. It keeps socialist values (equality, community, democracy, freedom) and the view that capitalism is flawed, but drops the labour theory of value, dialectics and the classical theory of revolution, and rejects Marx's reluctance to design socialist institutions. Its authors favour democratic, often market-based socialism, rejecting central planning and one-party statism.
scope: The September Group strand named by the SEP entry: G. A. Cohen, John Roemer and Jon Elster as founders, with Erik Olin Wright, Adam Przeworski and Philippe Van Parijs. Answers rest on the SEP account of the school, on Roemer's 1985 essay and on Wright's own books and essays, which the SEP cites as analytical Marxist work. Cohen's Why Not Socialism?, Roemer's A Future for Socialism and Elster's Making Sense of Marx were not available. Authors the SEP calls 'analytical Marxist' only in passing, and Marx himself, are not used.

missingStatements.text: Capitalism is unjust mainly because productive assets are very unequally owned, not because workers' labour is stolen.

notes: Statements searched in the sources by theme: economy (planning, markets, ownership, wages, basic income, taxation, inheritance), government (democracy, the state, parties, electoral rules, campaign finance, revolution and reform), world (imperialism, militarism), liberty (freedom, self-ownership), culture and ecology (consumerism, environment, gender and race in Wright's critique), technology and history. Most statements have no position in these sources and are null. The school's authors split on basic income, on the role of wages and profit-seeking firms, and on the primacy thesis of historical materialism. Wright's real-utopia proposals (citizens' assemblies, second chambers, democracy cards, participatory budgets) are his proposals, not school tenets, and are not answered from. The Why Not Socialism? Crooked Timber post and Wikipedia are not cited for any answer. If the audit fails the uncertainty rule, that is the honest result: the sources reachable here do not cover the school's positions on all lines. Lines the validator names (racial equality / ethnonationalism, nationalism, secularism / theocracy, minority rights, pluralism / authoritarianism, foreign policy) were searched in the SEP entry, Roemer 1985 and Wright's Compass Points and Envisioning Real Utopias chapters (race, gender, religion, nation, empire, minorities); the school's sources address them only as aspects of capitalist critique (militarism and imperialism, democracy), which settle none of those statements.
